questions.q: What primarily drives a decoherence (idle) error, as opposed to a gate error?
options: Elapsed time -- decoherence accumulates continuously via T1/T2 physics regardless of whether an operation is actively being applied to the qubit
The number of control wires connected to the qubit
The specific programming language used to write the quantum circuit
The physical temperature of the room the quantum computer sits in, independent of the refrigeration system
questions.explain: Decoherence/idle error is driven by elapsed time and T1/T2 physics (as established in Lesson 1's decayProb = 1 − e^(−t/T1)) -- it accrues whether or not a gate is actively being executed.

questions.q: What two specific causes does the lesson give for gate errors?
options: Control pulse miscalibration and crosstalk between neighboring qubits
T1 relaxation and T2 dephasing
Room temperature fluctuations and cosmic ray strikes
Software compiler bugs and network latency
questions.explain: The lesson identifies control pulse miscalibration (imprecisely shaped or amplitude-miscalibrated pulses) and crosstalk (a pulse meant for one qubit bleeding into a neighbor) as the specific causes of gate errors, distinct from the T1/T2-driven idle errors covered in Lesson 1.

questions.q: How does gate error typically scale as a circuit grows, in contrast to decoherence error?
options: Gate error scales roughly with the number of gate operations applied, roughly independent of each gate's individual duration, while decoherence error scales with total elapsed time
Gate error scales with elapsed time exactly the same way decoherence error does, with no distinction between the two
Gate error decreases as more gates are added to a circuit
Gate error only occurs in circuits with fewer than 10 gates total
questions.explain: The lesson's core distinction is that gate error scales with gate count (roughly constant per application) while decoherence error scales with total elapsed time -- two different scaling laws that both need to be tracked.

questions.q: Using the lesson's example of a fixed ~1×10⁻³ per-gate error budget compared against the Lesson 1 decoherence table, at a 20 ns gate duration which error source dominates?
options: Gate error dominates, since ~1×10⁻³ is larger than the roughly 2×10⁻⁴ decoherence probability at 20 ns
Decoherence error dominates by several orders of magnitude at 20 ns
The two error sources are always exactly equal at every gate duration
Neither error source is present at 20 ns gate durations
questions.explain: At 20 ns, decoherence probability is only about 1.9998×10⁻⁴, well below a ~1×10⁻³ fixed gate-error floor -- so at short gate durations, gate error can dominate total error, while decoherence catches up as gate time grows toward 1000 ns.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say quantum circuit design has to track both the per-gate error rate and T1/T2, rather than optimizing for just one?
options: Because whichever error source actually dominates depends on the specific hardware and circuit -- a circuit with few slow gates may be decoherence-dominated, while one with many fast gates may be gate-error-dominated, so reducing total error requires addressing whichever source is actually larger
Because T1/T2 and gate error are mathematically identical quantities and tracking both is redundant but harmless
Because only gate error matters in practice and T1/T2 can safely be ignored
Because only decoherence matters in practice and gate error can safely be ignored
questions.explain: The lesson explains that neither error source can be ignored -- which one dominates depends on gate speed and count for the specific hardware and circuit, so effective error-correction engineering has to account for both budgets together.
